airspace-over-states.essay:
The air over a country counts as part of that country in much the same way its land does. A government decides who may fly through it, on what terms, and when they must come down. The idea of founding a separate place in the sky over someone else's land therefore starts in a difficult position, and it helps to see how this rule came about.

An old common-law saying, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, held that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. Aircraft made that saying impractical for private owners. In United States v. Causby, a 1946 decision of the American Supreme Court, a family with 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, complained about military planes passing low over their chicken farm. The end of the runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. The Court wrote that the old doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway, because otherwise every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. The family kept a narrower claim, because flights low enough to interfere with the use of the land could still count as taking their property, which requires payment. A landowner therefore cannot sell or give away the sky above a plot, because a landowner does not hold it.

Governments kept for themselves what private owners lost. The main treaty is the Chicago Convention, signed by 52 states in Chicago on 7 December 1944 and in force since 4 April 1947, the day the International Civil Aviation Organization began work. That organization is the UN agency for civil flying, and it has 193 member countries by its own count. Article 1 says every country has complete and exclusive sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the airspace above its territory. The rule continues one in the 1919 Paris Convention on air travel. Article 2 says territory means land and the coastal waters next to it. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, confirms in Article 2(2) that a coastal country's authority also covers the air above its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast.

No treaty says how high this authority goes. Later agreements have not settled it either, so balloon flights, space planes and proposals for floating cities keep raising the same question. A founder cannot rely on that gap, because governments act at heights they can reach. On 4 February 2023, American F-22 fighters shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon off South Carolina. US officials put it at 60,000 to 65,000 feet, about 20 kilometres, above US territorial waters. China called the action unlawful force against a civil aircraft, and the United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. An analysis from Leiden Law School reasoned that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the treaty, and that at 20 kilometres it was in airspace.

The rest of the treaty shows how much a government can control. Article 6 says scheduled international flights need permission from each country flown over or landed in. Article 5 gives unscheduled flights more freedom, but only to aircraft of countries that have joined the treaty, and even then the country below may require the aircraft to land. Article 8 says pilotless aircraft need special permission. Article 9 lets a country close certain areas for military need or public safety. Article 12 says each country enforces flight rules over its territory, and also for aircraft carrying its registration marks wherever they are.

Suppose a group builds a large airship and declares it an independent nation while it floats over Kansas. The first question from any official is which country registered it. Under Articles 17 to 20, an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it, may be registered in one country only, is registered under that country's law, and must display that country's marks. The group's own register would mean nothing here, because the treaty counts only registers of member countries. If the airship stays unregistered, it appears to have no standing under the treaty at all. If the group registers it with the United States, it has accepted American rules on board. Under Articles 29 and 31, an aircraft in international flight must also carry a certificate of airworthiness, meaning an official finding that it is safe to fly, and its crew must hold licences. Those papers come from the registering country.

Moving to another country does not help, because the same problem repeats at each border. Cloud Nine, the floating spheres that the architect Buckminster Fuller and his partner Shoji Sadao drew around 1960, were meant to drift. Several thousand people would have lived inside spheres a mile wide. Nothing was built and no government was consulted, but under the Leiden reasoning a drifting city would need consent from every country below it. Loon, the internet balloon project owned by Google's parent company, shows what that means in practice. It flew about 20 kilometres up with no people aboard and a large company behind it. It signed a contract with Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's approval. Because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with neighbouring Uganda. No country had to challenge Loon, because it asked each one first.

Other problems would arrive in a rough order. A self-declared flying state could not win landing rights, since those depend on a member country standing behind the aircraft. It could rely on planes registered elsewhere, which brings that country's rules along. Radio use needs a licence. Fuel, repairs and food have to come from the ground, which means from an airport in some country, under that country's law. Passports fail as well, because the codes for issuing countries trace back to UN lists. Joining the civil aviation organization requires being a UN member or winning four-fifths of its Assembly with UN approval. Taxes follow the person. The United States taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, as the Supreme Court held in Cook v. Tait in 1924, so an American in the air would still file a return. A person hurt or accused of a crime on board would be dealt with under the law of the registering country or the country below.

A common misunderstanding is that a government must physically reach a craft before its law applies. The treaty works the other way round. The authority exists already, and the fighter jets are only one way of enforcing it. Another is that buying land brings the sky above it. Causby shows that it brings only the protection from low flights that interfere with the land.

The workable version is an ordinary aircraft or airship, built and flown with the permission of the country below and registered under its rules. Residents could agree private rules among themselves by contract, in the way members of a club do, and that is about as far as self-rule can go. The same government that grants permission can withdraw it or order the craft down, and the arrangement lasts only while it agrees. Estimates for this zone reflect that position. Building and flying are possible, while the chance of holding any independent status over a country's own land and coastal waters is very low, because Article 1 leaves no legal room for it.

airspace-over-high-seas.essay:
People often say that the country below owns the air. That statement is true over land and coastal waters, and it leaves out four things. No country holds authority over the air above the high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, which is about 58.6% of the sea surface. The air over Antarctica has no settled authority. No treaty sets the upper limit of airspace. An exclusive economic zone gives no airspace rights either. That zone, usually called the EEZ, is the belt up to 200 nautical miles from a coast where the coastal country controls resources. Only the territorial sea, up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, carries the air above it into the country's territory.

The rule comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Article 87(1)(b) says every country is free to fly over the high seas, and Article 58(1) applies the same freedom over the EEZ. Article 135 adds that the rules for the deep seabed, which the treaty calls the Area, do not change the legal status of the air above it. A country that controls the fish or the oil below therefore gains no right to shut the sky above them.

Antarctica works differently. The Antarctic Treaty governs the continent south of 60 degrees South, and its Article IV freezes the claims that seven countries have made to slices of the continent. Countries that do not recognize a claim therefore appear able to dispute whether the air above a claimed sector counts as the claimant's airspace. This is an interpretation, because the treaty does not address authority over airspace.

Freedom to fly here is a freedom held by countries, so it reaches a person through an aircraft that belongs to a country. Everything else follows from that. The Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, says in Articles 17 to 20 that an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it, may be on one register only, and must display that country's marks. Article 12 says each country must make sure that aircraft carrying its marks follow the rules wherever they are, and it adds that "over the high seas, the rules in force shall be those established under this Convention." The sky over the open ocean therefore has flight rules even though no country owns it. Those rules are the standards of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying.

Criminal law is handled by a second treaty. The Tokyo Convention, signed on 14 September 1963, applies to offences committed on board an aircraft in flight, including over the high seas or any other area outside every country's territory. It leaves out state aircraft used for military, customs or police work. It gives power over those offences to the state of registration, meaning the country where the aircraft is listed, and each party must make sure its law provides for this. A commander, the crew and in some cases passengers may act to prevent offences, and the commander may put an offender off the aircraft or hand them to the authorities on landing. Other countries generally may not interfere with an aircraft in flight to enforce their criminal law, with some exceptions. The arrangement resembles the rule for ships, which fall under the law of the country whose flag they fly. An aircraft flying over water no state owns therefore carries one country's legal system with it, and a registered flying platform would too.

Suppose a group builds a large long-range aircraft, stays over the middle of the Pacific, and declares that no country's law applies on board. The first problem comes before takeoff. The aircraft has to leave from an airport in some country, which will ask for its registration and its safety papers. If the group registers it, the registering country's law applies inside it, and a fight or a theft on board goes to that country's courts. If the group does not register it, it has no right to enter any country's airspace. Article 5 of the Chicago Convention gives its flight rights only to aircraft of countries that have joined, so an aircraft with no country has none of them.

That leads to the second problem, which is physical. Every aircraft has to take off and land somewhere. Fuel and maintenance force landings in a country, and on landing the crew and the craft are under that country's law. Residents of such a place would meet the same difficulties as anyone else who lands, including passports with no country code on the lists that border systems use. Food, spare parts and medical care all come through an airport in some country, under its rules on who may enter.

The third problem is that some countries reach out past their own airspace. An air defense identification zone is a stretch of sky beyond a country's airspace in which that country, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report. The United States created the first on 27 December 1950, during the Korean War, because it wanted early warning of a Soviet air attack. About 20 countries and regions now have such zones, including Canada, India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom. American policy applies its zone only to commercial aircraft intending to enter American airspace. On 23 November 2013 China declared a zone over the East China Sea, with reporting duties as far as 300 miles from its territorial waters and over islands Japan controls. Japan warned of unpredictable events, the United States objected, and South Korea expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. Legal writers disagree about these zones. One view holds that declaring one breaks no law, and another says they conflict with freedom of navigation in international airspace. No treaty authorises them, and Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore noted in 2014 that global conventions do not expressly forbid them either. A long-staying craft near one of these coasts should expect to be asked to identify itself.

The law of the sea treaty extends its piracy rules to aircraft, so under Articles 101 and 105 a private aircraft may be seized for piracy. Under Article 110(4), military aircraft may stop and inspect a suspect ship, which is called the right of visit. Taxes on an American citizen continue under Cook v. Tait, the 1924 Supreme Court case on worldwide income. Treaties could not be signed either, because a document signed by an unrecognized place would look to other countries like a private paper.

Two misunderstandings are common here. One is that a place no country owns is a place no country's law reaches. The law arrives on board with the registration and travels with the passengers. The other is that the freedom to fly over the sea is a personal right. Article 87 gives it to countries, and an individual uses it through a country's register.

The workable version is an ordinary registered aircraft flying over open water, with residents following private agreements under the law of the registering country. A permanently airborne self-governing craft has not been built and would still need to be on a register. This zone gets a higher legal estimate than the air over land because no coastal country holds title here. The estimates for holding on stay low because of the landings, the registration and the identification zones, and the chance of recognition by other countries is estimated at close to nothing.

airborne-habitats.essay:
The idea of living permanently in the air appears in films and in architects' drawings, and it has never been done. Nobody lives on a flying platform today. To understand why, it helps to look at the machines that come closest and at the rules they already answer to.

The closest machines are called high-altitude platforms. These are uncrewed aircraft or airships meant to stay very high up for weeks or years, usually to carry radio equipment, so that they work a little like a very low satellite. The International Telecommunication Union, or ITU, is the UN agency that coordinates radio use, and its definition is the nearest thing to a legal description of these craft. Paragraph 1.66A of its Radio Regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a radio station on an object at 20 to 50 kilometres up, at a specified nominal fixed point relative to the Earth. That wording covers radio use only. It says nothing about who owns the air at that height, and it treats the platform as a piece of radio equipment.

Those heights lie above normal traffic. In the United States, Class A airspace, the controlled airspace used by airliners, ends at 60,000 feet, about 18 kilometres, and these platforms fly above it. The published page from the Federal Aviation Administration, the US aviation regulator, does not say how they are regulated up there. Above Class A there is no special legal zone. Air over a country falls under that country's rules, and no treaty sets the height where this ends. No case of anyone claiming a flying nation appears in the published descriptions of these programs.

The history of the hardware explains the physical side. Helios, a NASA solar aircraft, reached 96,863 feet on 13 August 2001 and broke up in flight in 2003. The Airbus Zephyr, a solar drone, can fly for 64 days. Facebook's Aquila drone was halted in 2018, Google's Loon balloons ended in 2021, and Titan Aerospace's Solara was shut down by 2017. Other craft named in this height band include the BAE PHASA-35 and the Kea Atmos Mk1. All of these carry equipment. None carries a person to live on.

Stratobus is the project most like a long-stay habitat, and it shows how slowly such a thing moves. It is a robotic airship designed by the French company Thales Alenia Space to hover about 20 kilometres up. In 2015 the design was 100 metres long, weighed about 5 tons and could carry 250 kilograms of equipment for five years. The company expected a couple of days on the ground each year for maintenance. It planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020, and neither date was met. By 2025 it was described as 142 metres long, the company had started building two reduced-scale test models, and the aim was to be ready for use by 2031. The carrying limit matters here. A payload of 250 kilograms on a craft that large is less than the weight of three or four adults, before counting food, water, air supply or walls. No plans for people aboard have been reported.

Sky Cruise is the famous picture of the opposite end. It is an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022, based on a design by art director Tony Holmsten drawn more than a decade earlier. It shows a nuclear-powered flying hotel carrying up to 5,000 people and staying in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving on jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili suggested that small reactors expected in the 2030s might power it. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and he himself stressed that it is only a concept. No such aircraft has been built.

Suppose someone did build a crewed platform and wanted to run it as an independent place. The bumps would come in this order. Before takeoff, the craft needs safety certification and flight permission. Stratobus's makers said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, and that was for a craft with nobody aboard. Certificates come from a country, and that country's aviation authority answers for the craft. In practice, a platform answers to the aviation and radio authorities that certify it. An aircraft must be registered with a country to have legal standing under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on international civil flying, and the registering country's rules follow it.

Next come radio frequencies. A platform needs them to talk to the ground and to run any business, and frequency assignments reach the ITU through a member country, which puts that member's regulator in charge. A group with no member country behind it would have no one to file for it. Then comes the question of where the craft is. Over a country, it is in that country's air and subject to its orders. Over open ocean, no one owns the air, but the craft still carries its register's law.

After that come the physical limits. Even a platform designed for years in the air has to come down somewhere for maintenance, as Stratobus does for a couple of days a year. A place with people on it would have far greater needs, including food, water, medicine and a way to bring a sick person down. Each of those runs through an airfield in some country. Whoever controls that airfield controls the supply, which is the same weakness seen in Camp Barneo, the Arctic tourist camp that depended on Norwegian flights. Insurance, money and banking would then present the same problems as any other place outside a recognized state. A flying place with no recognized government could not license a bank, and its residents would remain citizens of their home countries, subject to their tax laws.

The business side has its own record. Several programs ended with large companies behind them, including Loon, which Alphabet closed in 2021 because it lacked a viable business. Those programs carried only equipment, with no food, water, air or medical care to pay for.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a height above airliner traffic is a height above the law. Class A ending at 60,000 feet only marks where one kind of air traffic control stops. In February 2023 American fighters shot down a Chinese balloon at about that height. The other is that a video of a flying city means someone is building one. Sky Cruise is an animation, and the design for it has not moved past that.

The workable version today is an uncrewed platform flown with a government's permission, carrying radio or observation equipment, on a register, using licensed frequencies. No crewed flight has been reported for these programs. A permanent home in the air remains unbuilt, and estimates for it are low on building, on law and on holding the position, because the craft would need a state's registration and somewhere to land or receive supplies.

floating-ice.essay:
Ice that floats in the sea is hard for the law to classify. A person can walk on it and build a hut, as on land, and it also moves with the currents and melts. Who owns a floating iceberg has no settled answer.

It helps to separate three kinds of floating ice. Sea ice forms when the ocean surface freezes. An ice shelf is a thick sheet of floating ice still attached to land, like those around Antarctica. An iceberg or ice island is a large piece that has broken off a glacier or shelf and drifts free.

Legal writers take three views of an iceberg floating free. The first says it belongs to no one, which lawyers call res nullius, so the first to take it may keep it, much as a fisherman keeps a fish. The second says it can be held under a claim by a country. The third says it is shared by all, which is called res communis, in the way the open sea is shared. In a 2022 article in the law journal Ius Novum, Mateusz Osiecki argues that an iceberg floating free in Antarctic waters is no country's property and sits on the high seas, so taking and towing it would probably not breach any country's territorial rights. That is one writer's reasoning, and no court has ruled on it.

Location adds another layer. The Antarctic Treaty, under its Article VI, covers everything south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, without taking away rights any country has on the high seas in that area. An ice shelf is therefore treated like part of Antarctica, with its frozen claims and its rules. A berg that has drifted north of that line is simply floating in the ocean. A towing ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. Osiecki notes that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has joined neither the Antarctic Treaty System nor the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, which leaves open how far those rules bind a UAE-flagged tow. He also sets out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty.

The one court that has come near this question did so after a killing. T-3, also called Fletcher's Ice Island, was a drifting iceberg in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as a staffed American research station from 1952 to 1978, with huts, a power plant and an airstrip. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla, armed with a borrowed rifle during a dispute over raisin wine, shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey. The island then lay in the Arctic sector Canada claimed, but Canada chose not to act and said this did not affect its claims. American officials flew Escamilla to Virginia and charged him, arguing that the ice was on the high seas and so within the special American law for crimes at sea. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law covered an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place. The conviction was overturned for other errors, and he was acquitted at a new trial. Congress did not settle the question until a change to federal law in 1984. The shooting on unclaimed ice did not fall outside all law. A national government took the suspect home, and the argument was about which statute applied.

Physically, the record shows that people can live on ice for weeks or years with heavy support, and never permanently. On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on a floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole. Four men lived there for nine months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, until icebreakers took them off in February 1938. From 1954, one to three stations ran each year. A typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years, until its floe reached the Greenland Sea, and North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. Some 800 people have drifted on these stations since 1937, with crews replaced each year. All were run by one government body, the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice thawed too fast. Russia therefore ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform in 2017, completed in August 2022, which ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024 and started NP-42 in 2024.

Antarctic ice has given its own warning. The iceberg A23a broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986 and carried off part of the Soviet base Druzhnaya I, which stood on that part of the shelf. Rusted debris from the base could still be seen in the ice in January 2025. A23a measured about 3,500 square kilometres in January 2025, when it was the largest iceberg in the world. By March 2026 it was down to 180 square kilometres, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so.

Suppose a private group sets up on a floe and declares it a country. The first thing it needs is an aircraft or ship, and the base for that is in some country. Camp Barneo shows what follows. It was a private tourist camp near the North Pole, founded in 2002 by the Russian Alexander Orlov, with visits from about $20,000. Because the ice keeps moving, it had to be rebuilt from nothing every April, and in 2007 winds pushed it at 0.8 kilometres an hour. Every trip from 2002 to 2017 started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, so it relied on Norway. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight ban, which it later lifted. A Russia-Ukraine dispute stopped tourist flights in 2019, COVID-19 cancelled two seasons, Russia's invasion of Ukraine ended plans for 2022, and a 2024 season was cancelled. The camp last operated in 2018. No one needs to board the ice to stop a camp, because restricting the flights is enough.

The other bumps follow from that. A camp without a government behind it has no icebreaker to rescue it when the floe cracks. Its residents remain citizens of their home countries, with the same taxes and the same criminal law. It has no fixed address for a bank, an insurer or a land title, since the ground itself drifts and may melt. The Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty that defines a state, asks for a defined territory, which a melting floe struggles to offer.

Building a stronger iceberg has been tried on paper. Project Habakkuk was a British wartime plan by Geoffrey Pyke for a floating airbase made of ice. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that natural icebergs have too little surface above water for an airstrip and can roll over. The idea moved on to pykrete, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp, and a ship 600 metres long. Pykrete sagged unless cooled to minus 16 degrees Celsius, the estimate rose from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and the board called the ship impractical in December 1943. The UAE Iceberg Project, announced in 2017 by Abdulla Alsheni at an estimated $100 to 150 million, aimed only to tow a berg from near Heard Island to Fujairah for water, and no tow is known to have taken place.

The workable version is a temporary camp or research station with a country or a large company behind it, supplied by air or ship, lasting a season to a few years. It gives no title and no self-rule. Estimates put the chance of building a lasting place very low, while the legal estimate is moderate only because the law is unsettled.

add_sources.t: United States v. Escamilla, 467 F.2d 341 (4th Cir. 1972)

new-land.essay:
Now and then a volcano or an earthquake pushes new ground above the sea, or a river delta piles up a sandbar. This looks like an opening, because the ground is brand new and no one has ever lived on it. Many people assume that new land belongs to whoever gets there first. In practice the answer depends on where the ground rises and how long it lasts.

Start with the old rule on unclaimed land. For centuries a country could gain land that belonged to no one, called terra nullius, by actually occupying and governing it. In the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928, between the United States and the Netherlands, the arbitrator Max Huber held that discovery alone does not settle ownership, and that a continuous and peaceful display of state authority wins over a mere first finding. That method was one used by countries. A private person who plants a flag gets nothing from it directly, and a country must then keep governing the place.

Most new ground never reaches that question, because the sea around it is already spoken for. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, Article 2 gives a coastal country full authority over its territorial sea, the belt reaching up to 12 nautical miles from its coast, and over the seabed below. A volcano that surfaces there rises on ground that country already holds. New land is therefore almost always the property of the country whose waters it rises in. Zalzala Koh shows the simple case. It appeared off Pakistan on 24 September 2013, within hours of a 7.7-magnitude earthquake, about 2 kilometres from shore near Gwadar. It lay inside Pakistan's territorial sea, so no one else could have claimed it.

Further out the law becomes less clear. Between 12 and 200 nautical miles lies the exclusive economic zone, the belt where the coastal country controls resources, and its rights to the seabed there concern resources and do not amount to full ownership. Article 60 gives the coastal country control of artificial islands in that zone, but it does not directly address a natural island that appears. A coastal country would very likely claim such an island at once, but the treaty does not spell out the answer. Beyond national zones, Article 137 says no country may claim or take over any part of the deep seabed, and whether that reaches a natural island rising from it has not been tested. Land rising from a seabed no one holds has only one tested case, and the land sank before any claim succeeded.

That case is Graham Island. It rose about 30 kilometres south of Sicily in July 1831. By 17 July a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, had landed and planted an oar to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. By 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy had claimed it for Britain and named it after Sir James Graham. King Ferdinand II sent a warship and called it Ferdinandea, a French geologist named it Julia, and Spain declared an interest. At its largest it was about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high. It was loose ash, and by 17 December officials reported no trace, so that it was gone by January 1832 and the dispute lapsed unsettled. Its summit now lies about 6 metres under water, and when it stirred in 2000 and 2002, Italians placed a flag and a plaque on the bank to head off future claims.

The speed of government is the first lesson of these cases. In 1963 the eruption that made Surtsey began off the south coast of Iceland on 14 November. On 6 December three French journalists from Paris Match landed, stayed about 15 minutes and jokingly claimed it for France, and Iceland immediately said it was Icelandic. In 1965, while the eruption was still going on, Iceland declared the island a nature reserve so that scientists could watch life arrive. The eruption ended on 5 June 1967, with the highest point at 174 metres. Hard lava had capped the ash, so the island lasted. Only a few scientists may land, and no one has been able to settle there. Japan's Nishinoshima, about 940 kilometres south-southeast of Tokyo, went the same way. A fishing boat reported smoke on 30 May 1973, the Japan Coast Guard flew over that day, and the new land merged with an island Japan already held, as did more ground from 2013 onward.

The second lesson is that the ground rarely lasts. Graham Island lasted about six months and Zalzala Koh about three years, sinking 3 metres in its first month and gone by the end of 2016. Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai, in Tonga, joined in 2015, and the merged island reached 149 metres and acquired ferns and seabirds before the eruption of January 2022 destroyed most of it, leaving small remnants. Fonuafoʻou, whose name means new land, appeared on 14 October 1885, grew through several eruptions, collapsed in 1949 and is now 17 metres under water. Anything built on such ground would be lost with it.

Sandbars add a dispute of their own. South Talpatti, which India called New Moore, formed in the Bay of Bengal after the cyclone of November 1970. It never rose above 2 metres. India and Bangladesh both claimed it, because the border follows the main channel of the nearby river, and India reportedly raised its flag in 1981. It had gone by about March 2010. In the Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration, a panel of judges chosen to settle the dispute drew the sea boundary in 2014 and left the site of the vanished island on the Indian side. The dispute ran for decades between two governments, over ground that no longer existed when it ended.

Suppose a group does get to a new island first, in waters that no one has clearly claimed. It lands by boat, which comes from a port, and plants a flag. Within days a government asks what it is doing, as happened in 1831 and 1963. If it stays, it has to haul in all its water and food, since new ash holds neither. Its huts stand on loose material that waves wear down. A government can remove it, as Tonga did at Minerva, or declare a reserve, as Iceland did at Surtsey. Its home countries still tax its members and can prosecute them. No bank or insurer has a legal owner to deal with, because nobody can show title.

Three misunderstandings are common. The first is that a person can claim new land by landing on it, when that method belongs to countries. The second is that building up a reef or sandbar makes an island. Article 121(1) says an island is land that formed naturally, has water all round it and stays above water at high tide. Article 60(8) says artificial islands are not islands in law, with no territorial sea and no effect on sea boundaries. The Republic of Minerva, whose backers piled sand on a South Pacific reef in 1971, was claimed and taken over by Tonga in 1972. The third is that any island brings a large sea zone with it. Under Article 121(3), rocks that cannot support people living there or an economy of their own get no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf, the seabed rights a coast normally carries.

There is no real workable version for a founder. The realistic options are visiting as a scientist or tourist, where permitted, or watching from a small plane as visitors do at Surtsey. Estimates are low for building, because new ground washes away, and low for holding it, because a government arrives quickly.

high-seas.essay:
The high seas are the part of the ocean beyond every country's coastal zones. The ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface, according to the US agency NOAA. About 58.6% of the sea surface is high seas, by the calculation of MarineRegions, a marine geography database. Parliamentarians for Global Action, an advocacy group, puts the high seas at 43% of Earth's surface, and another page on its site says about half. The figures depend on the definition used. Either way, this is the largest area of the planet that no government owns, which is why people who want to start a new society keep looking at it.

The rules come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. It has 172 members and has been in effect since 16 November 1994. The United States is outside it. Article 86 applies the high-seas rules to all sea outside a country's exclusive economic zone (its coastal resource zone, up to 200 nautical miles or about 370 km), its territorial sea (the belt next to its coast), its internal waters and the waters between the islands of an island nation. Article 87 says the high seas are open to all countries. The listed freedoms include sailing, flying over, laying cables and building artificial islands, that last one "subject to Part VI", the continental shelf rules, and "permitted under international law".

Two points in that wording are often missed. Article 87 words these freedoms as belonging to countries and does not grant them to private people, so a person uses them through a country. And Article 89 says no country may validly claim any part of the high seas as its own. A new state could not gain a piece of this sea by occupying it, because the rule against claims applies to every state.

The high seas are governed through ships, and each ship carries one country's law with it. Article 92 says a ship sails under one flag only and answers to that flag country on the high seas. Article 110 sets out when a warship may board a foreign ship, other than a warship or government ship. It may do so if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality. Having no flag is the main obstacle here, because Article 110(1)(d) lets a warship come aboard to check. The article speaks of ships, so applying it to a fixed structure is an inference and has not been settled.

Suppose a group tows a barge out 300 nautical miles and declares a republic. The first decision is whether to register. Physically, the group would tow or sail a vessel or platform out and bring supplies from a port, which puts it under that port's law on each visit. Legally, it would register with a willing country, which means accepting that country's law on board. If it declares its own flag, other countries will see no flag at all. The people on board also remain nationals of their home countries, and a country such as the US claims power to prosecute crimes committed by or against its nationals in "any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation" (18 USC 7(7)). Americans still file tax returns under Cook v. Tait, the 1924 Supreme Court case on worldwide income. Giving up US citizenship without holding another nationality leaves a person stateless.

The next question is the seabed. Anchoring means touching the bottom, and the bottom has its own rules. Beyond 200 nautical miles, the seabed may still be part of another country's extended continental shelf, the seabed a country controls beyond the usual limit under Article 76, or part of the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority. Anchoring there raises separate questions.

A newer treaty adds paperwork for countries that have joined it. The BBNJ Agreement, on marine life in areas outside any country's control, was adopted on 19 June 2023 and took effect on 17 January 2026. It had 145 signing countries and 105 members on the UN status page in November 2026, and its first Conference of the Parties, the members' meeting, is set for 11 to 22 January 2027. Under Articles 3 and 28, members must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control there before allowing them. It also adds rules on genetic resources from sea life, over which no country may claim authority (Article 11), on marine protected areas, and on help for countries to build their capacity.

Then comes money. Published estimates start at about $50 million for a small deep-sea platform and reach billions for a city. Residents would need a bank, and international payments move between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A place with no banking law and no supervisor gives those banks no one to rely on, so a wire transfer cannot arrive. Selling shares in a future country can count as selling securities, as Lazarus Long found in 1999 when US regulators sued him over $350 million in bonds for a Caribbean nation called New Utopia. He had raised $24,000. Medical care means going ashore, and a nearby captain must rescue people in danger under Article 98, after which they land in someone else's country.

The real cases show where projects stop. Aisland is the only one here where people lived on the water, and its anchorage in the Persian Gulf was not on the high seas. Samuele Landi, an Italian businessman sentenced in his absence to 14 years for fraud, lived on an 800-ton barge about 30 miles off Dubai with shipping containers for quarters. He planned to move to the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean, and hoped for about twenty barges by 2028. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two. Landi and two employees died, and no state had ever challenged him.

The Seasteading Institute, founded in 2008 by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman with $500,000 from Peter Thiel, hoped for a seastead by 2014 and missed the date. It then turned to working inside a country's waters and signed a non-binding memorandum with French Polynesia in 2017. That government pulled out in 2018. Eric Klien's Atlantis Project of 1993, or Oceania, published a full constitution before building anything, needed about $1 billion, and collapsed in April 1994 for lack of interest. Its site, 50 miles off Panama, was in fact inside a coastal resource zone. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman, failed to buy land from Kiribati and the Gambia and announced Arca Noë in 2020 for what he called neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. No structure has been reported.

The commonest misunderstanding is that no owner means no law. Another is that a declaration is enough. The tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty, ask for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and open water gives no territory to define.

The most workable version is a registered vessel under a real flag, with residents agreeing private rules by contract. This place has a better legal position than most, because no coastal state holds title, and the estimates reflect that. The estimates for holding it stay low because of the costs, the sea and Article 110, and recognition by other countries is estimated at well under one percent.

stratosphere-near-space.essay:
Above the heights where airliners fly and below the heights where satellites can stay in orbit lies a band of thin air that has no agreed legal name. People call parts of it the stratosphere, a layer of the atmosphere, and "near space", the band above normal aircraft and below orbit. It attracts people because it seems to sit between two legal systems. No treaty sets special rules for it, and that gap is the place to begin.

Two treaties meet here without touching. The Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, says in Article 1 that countries hold full authority over the air above their territory, and it states no height limit. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article II that no country can take over outer space, but it does not say where outer space begins. The situation resembles two neighbouring properties with no survey of the boundary between them. Over a country, this height is treated in practice as that country's airspace. Over the high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, the same freedom to fly applies as at lower heights.

People have tried to draw the boundary. The UN's space committee, COPUOS, has considered where to draw the line between air and space since 1967 without agreeing, and some countries oppose defining a line at all. Legal writers describe two camps. The spatial camp wants a fixed height, and the functional camp would classify an object by what it does. The figure most often used is the Kármán line at 100 km, named after the engineer Theodore von Kármán. It is a reference point that has not been agreed in law, according to the Library of Congress. FAI, the body that keeps air-sport records, uses it to separate aeronautics from astronautics. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in their space laws, and the US has endorsed 100 km as the point where its Air Force's and Space Force's areas of responsibility divide, according to a 2025 UN submission. The US armed forces also call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 km, an astronaut, and the astronomer Jonathan McDowell argued in 2018 for 80 km as better suited to the physics. Other proposals include 110 km (UN paper A/AC.105/L.168), and 120 km and 160 km for the top of near space. Another would set the boundary at the lowest point a satellite can reach in orbit. A UN submission states that national airspace has functionally not been legislated beyond 400,000 feet, about 122 km. That language comes from a draft treaty by the International Association for the Advancement of Space Safety, and it is not law.

The lower edge is also blurred. New Zealand defines high altitude as starting from flight level 600, an aviation measure of about 60,000 feet. Most aircraft fly below it, according to the Jakarta Post, citing the International Civil Aviation Organization. A UN submission puts flight level 600 at approximately 18 km, while the Jakarta Post says 20 km. The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for radio coordination, treats stations at 20 to 50 km as high-altitude platforms, but that definition concerns radio only.

A founder might think of this band as unclaimed. Events in 2023 show that governments do not treat it that way at the heights a balloon can reach. On 4 February 2023, American F-22 fighters shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon off South Carolina. US officials said it was between 60,000 and 65,000 feet, about 20 km up, above US territorial waters. China called this unlawful force against a civil aircraft, and the United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. An analysis from Leiden Law School reasoned that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the Chicago Convention, and that at 20 km it was in airspace and not in outer space. If it was a civil aircraft, Article 3 bis of the treaty and customary law limit the use of weapons against it. If it was a state aircraft, the treaty does not apply and the general law on steps taken in response to another state's breach does. Article 1 applies at whatever height a country can reach.

Loon shows the peaceful route. It carried mobile network equipment about 20 km up on balloons, steered by choosing among the high-altitude winds. It started in 2011 at Google's experimental lab. It signed with Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's approval. Because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with Uganda. No country had to challenge it, because it asked first. Alphabet closed it in 2021 for lack of a viable business.

Suppose someone wanted to station a crewed platform at 30 km and declare independence. Launches and balloon flights begin on a country's soil, so the first letter would come from a national aviation authority, and a launch licence may also be needed where a rocket is involved. Balloons and high-altitude platforms need a launch site, an entry on a register and radio frequencies from a country. Under the treaty the craft takes the nationality of its register. Frequencies are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, so that member's regulator is in charge. Above the band where normal aircraft fly, a person cannot breathe the outside air, so the platform needs a sealed cabin and must carry its air, water and food, which are brought up from a country below. Sickness or a leak means coming down, in whichever country lies below or across the winds.

The hardware is far from this stage. JP Aerospace, a volunteer American group founded by John Powell, wants an inhabited floating base called a Dark Sky Station as a step towards orbit. The Register described mile-wide platforms at 140,000 feet, about 43 km, and Powell described a full-size station two miles across in 2004. So far it has built a 175-foot airship called Ascender for about $500,000 and flown an uncrewed craft called Tandem at 95,085 feet on 22 October 2011. Nobody has lived on any of it, and the group makes no claim to sovereignty. A station at that height would still sit below both the 80 km and 100 km lines. Cloud Nine, the mile-wide floating spheres drawn by Buckminster Fuller and Shoji Sadao around 1960, remained a photocollage.

Three misunderstandings recur. The first is that the lack of a treaty height leaves an empty gap, when it actually leaves each country free to say the air is its own and to act where it can. The second is that the Kármán line is law. Some bodies and some national laws use it, and no treaty does. The third is that a position over the open ocean escapes all this. The freedom to fly there belongs to countries, and the craft still needs a register, as any aircraft does, and a place to start and finish its flight.

The workable version is an uncrewed balloon or platform flown under a national licence with the consent of the countries below. No self-governing station at this height has been found, and no platform here carries people for long stays. A crewed version would have the legal status of a registered aircraft. Estimates are low on building and on holding such a place, and recognition is estimated at close to nothing.

leo.essay:
Low Earth orbit is the band of space closest to the planet, under 2,000 km up according to the European Space Agency. The International Space Station (ISS) circles there, along with most satellites. Because it can be reached with rockets that are already for sale, and because no country owns it, this is the first place in space that people imagine settling. The law here was written for governments, long before any private station.

During the Cold War, governments worried that a rival might claim the Moon or put weapons in orbit, and they wrote the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, in 1967. It had 118 member countries and 23 that had signed without joining as at 1 January 2026, up from 116 a year earlier with the addition of Latvia and Malaysia. Article I says space is free for all countries to use. Article II says no country may take it over by claiming authority, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Read alone, those two articles look like an opening for founders.

The next articles take that opening away. Article VI says countries answer for private space activities, which need permission and continuing oversight from an appropriate member country. Article VII says launching countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage. Article VIII says the country that registers an object keeps legal power and control over it and anyone on board. Article IX says countries must pay due attention to others and consult before causing harmful interference. So nobody can own the place, and every object in it falls under the legal system of some country on Earth, much as every ship on the high seas has a flag state.

Three more treaties fill in the details. The Registration Convention, on listing space objects, has 77 members. Under Articles II and IV, the launching country registers each object and reports its details to the UN. Only launching countries and qualifying international organizations run such registers, so a private person appears to have no way to register alone. The Liability Convention, on who pays for space damage, has 100 members plus 4 organizations that accept it by declaration. Under Articles II and III, a launching country must pay for damage on Earth or to aircraft whether or not it was at fault, and elsewhere it pays only if it was at fault. The Rescue Agreement, on helping astronauts in distress, has 100 members plus 3 declarations. A country that can be billed for what its citizens launch has a reason to license them.

Suppose a group wants an independent orbital station. The first obstacle is on the ground, because no one can leave Earth without a launching country. That country must give permission, register the station and keep legal power over it. A US citizen launching from anywhere outside the US needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US aviation regulator, under 51 USC 50904. The licence requires insurance for harm to others, capped at $500 million or the most available at reasonable cost, and the government can block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. People on board must be told in writing that the government has not certified the vehicle, and US rules on occupant safety are largely on hold in a learning period set to end on January 1, 2028. A group would buy its launch from a licensed operator, under that licensing system.

The second step is radio. A station must talk to the ground, and radio contact needs a filing with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio coordination, through a member country. Under Articles 44 and 45 of the ITU Constitution, orbits and frequencies are limited natural resources and stations must not cause harmful interference. Swarm Technologies shows that this reaches past borders. The US regulator, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), refused in December 2017 to license its four tiny satellites, fearing they could not be tracked. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018 on an Indian rocket. It paid a $900,000 penalty and accepted a compliance plan. The foreign launch made no difference, because the company was American and its satellites signalled ground stations in Georgia. The FCC also fined Dish Network $150,000 in 2023 for leaving a satellite too low at the end of its life.

Flags of convenience, the practice of registering a ship in a country with light rules, have been proposed for space. The limit is that any launching state stays liable, so a cheap register cannot remove the liability of the country whose soil was used. No court has tested this.

Asgardia shows what a declaration achieves. Igor Ashurbeyli announced this self-declared space nation in 2016. On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia carried its 2.8 kg satellite, Asgardia-1, to orbit on a NASA-funded mission flown by US companies, and legal scholars pointed out that it stayed under US authority. It burned up on 12 September 2022 with no replacement reported. No one has ever lived there, and no state or UN body recognises it.

Money and supplies come next. The ISS costs about $3 billion a year to operate, according to NASA's Inspector General, and its crews still rely on delivered tanks, water and food. At about $3,246 per kg on a Falcon 9 rocket, food at 2.77 kg a day comes to about $3.3 million per person each year in launch costs alone. MirCorp, which leased the Russian station Mir and paid for its last crew in 2000, ran out of money and lost Mir when it was brought down in March 2001. Bigelow Aerospace put in $250 million of its founder's money and laid off all 88 staff in March 2020. Aurora Station offered 12-day stays at $9.5 million and closed without building anything. Vast's single-module Haven-1 had not been launched as of November 2026, with launch set for no earlier than the first quarter of 2027. Axiom Station, Orbital Reef and Starlab depend on NASA as main customer and funder, and none has flown or seeks self-government.

In the one place people live long-term, law on board is settled by treaty. The ISS Intergovernmental Agreement of 1998 lets each partner keep legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens. Under Article 22, a country may prosecute its own citizens, and if misconduct endangers another partner's citizen or module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country. A Crew Code of Conduct sets a chain of command.

Some ideas try to work inside this system. The ORBIS lease, discussed by Alexander Salter in 2019, is a model contract for a privately owned settlement whose residents accept rules by agreement. Article VI still requires a country's supervision, and no settlement is known to have used it. Cloud Constellation's SpaceBelt pitched orbiting data storage outside national rules, although European data law protects residents' data even when processed elsewhere, and no launch has been reported. Kessler syndrome, a chain reaction of collisions predicted by two NASA scientists in 1978, adds a physical limit, because one operator's debris endangers all others and no settlement can fence off its surroundings. A seriously ill resident has to be brought back to Earth, into some country, and the Rescue Agreement returns people to the launching authority, which a self-declared state appears unable to be.

The workable version is a privately owned station, licensed and registered by one country, with residents living under its law and under private contracts. Private tokens and house rules could work inside that frame without giving independence. Estimates put money and building higher than law and holding, and they put recognition at close to nothing.

How accurate were Musk's Falcon 9 and Starship per-kg claims (New Space Economy)

central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard.essay:
The Arctic has two very different places that a founder might think about, and it helps to keep them apart. One is the central Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, which is open sea covered by moving ice. The other is Svalbard, a group of real islands about twice the size of Belgium, where people from many countries can live without a visa. Neither place offers independence.

Begin with the ocean. It is high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, surrounded by the coastal resource zones of five countries, Canada, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Russia and the United States. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, applies there, and the same limits apply as on any high seas. No one may claim the water, and a vessel needs a flag or it can be boarded. There is also a treaty on fishing. The Agreement to Prevent Unregulated High Seas Fisheries in the Central Arctic Ocean was concluded at Ilulissat, Greenland, on 3 October 2018 and took effect for Canada on 25 June 2021. Under Articles 1 and 13 it covers the single area of high seas surrounded by those five countries and runs for 16 years, with five-year renewals. Its opening text says ice has generally covered this water all year, though the ice is shrinking.

The seabed below may not be free at all. Under Article 76 of UNCLOS, a coastal country's continental shelf, the seabed it controls for resources, can reach past 200 nautical miles within set limits. The seabed under the central Arctic can therefore belong to a coastal country and fall outside the international deep seabed. Russia's 2007 expedition shows how this works and how it does not. Two small Mir submarines planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the Pole, at 4,261 metres, under the expedition leader Artur Chilingarov. Canada's foreign minister Peter MacKay answered that this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory, and a US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-nautical-mile zones of the five coastal countries leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question, which is an unofficial figure. He said any country wanting that seabed has to build a scientific case under the treaty, and he called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim. A private flag would have no more effect. Greenpeace lowered its own flag to the same seabed in April 2013, with a capsule holding nearly three million signatures asking for a global sanctuary. The European Parliament has called for a sanctuary too, and none has been created.

Physically, the ocean is very hard to live on. It offers moving ice and no local supplies. The one legal test comes from a research camp. T-3, a drifting iceberg about 11 by 5 kilometres, was a staffed American station from 1952 to 1978. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey, during a dispute over raisin wine. The island lay within the sector Canada claimed, and Canada took no action. American officials flew him to Virginia and tried him under the special American law for crimes at sea. A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law applied there, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place, and it overturned the conviction for other trial errors. He was acquitted at a new trial. Congress settled the question of legal authority over such a place in 1984. Living on the ice therefore did not put anyone beyond a court.

Now turn to Svalbard. Until the 20th century it was terra nullius, land belonging to no state. Whalers and then miners from many countries worked there with almost no law, and disputes between miners and owners created demand for a government. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty was the answer, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925. It began with 14 parties and has 49 members as of 2026, according to Wikipedia. Article 1 recognizes Norway's "full and absolute sovereignty". Articles 2 and 3 give nationals of member countries equal rights to fishing, hunting, access, trade and mining, subject to local law. Article 8 says taxes must be spent on Svalbard itself, and mining rules cannot favor anyone. Article 9 says no naval base or fortification may be built. Russia uses its rights through its settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden, and about 2,500 people live on the islands.

Many people hear "no visa" and assume Svalbard is a kind of free zone. The Governor of Svalbard, Norway's local official, explains otherwise. Norway's Immigration Act does not apply there, so a foreigner needs no Norwegian visa or residence permit, though someone needing a Schengen visa must have one to travel through mainland Norway, and a double-entry visa to come back. Everyone must carry a valid travel document. Under Norway's rejection and expulsion regulations for Svalbard, people must have the means to live there, and the Governor may reject those who do not. This applies to Norwegians and foreigners alike. Those planning to come are advised to obtain work and housing first. Most housing belongs to employers, so it is hard to get housing without a job. The Norwegian state owns practically all land, and in practice it is not possible to buy a plot to build a home. Private boats and planes must send advance notice of passengers and crew. Living there gives no rights to govern. Norwegian law and the Governor apply. Under rules announced in 2022, non-Norwegians must have lived three years in a Norwegian municipality to vote or stand in Longyearbyen's local elections, and time on Svalbard does not count, which could affect over 700 of the 2,500 people there.

Suppose a group of friends moved to Longyearbyen, the main town, and announced a self-governing community. They would need jobs and homes from existing employers, and they could rent and trade like anyone else. Their declaration would have no effect, because 49 countries have recognized Norway's sovereignty in the treaty. If they could not support themselves, the Governor could send them away.

Older Arctic cases show what happens to those who try to take land. Norway itself tried in 1931 to occupy part of eastern Greenland, calling it Erik the Red's Land and arguing it belonged to no state. On 5 April 1933 the Permanent Court of International Justice ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. In 1921 Vilhjalmur Stefansson sent five settlers to Wrangel Island, north of Siberia, to claim it for Canada. A relief ship failed in 1922, three set out for Siberia and vanished, one died of scurvy, and Ada Blackjack survived alone until rescue in August 1923. A new party of 13 was removed by a Soviet ship in 1924, and its leader, Charles Wells, and two children died. Hans Island, a bare rock of 1.3 square kilometres, was divided peacefully by Canada, Denmark and Greenland on 14 June 2022 after decades in which each side raised flags and left gifts.

The workable version is simple and limited. An ordinary person from a member country can move to Svalbard, if they can support themselves, and live and do business under Norwegian law. In the central ocean, a registered ship or a government-backed camp is possible for short periods. The legal estimate for this zone is moderate because of those open rights, and the holding estimate is low because no one can govern there.

United States v. Escamilla, 467 F.2d 341 (4th Cir. 1972)

ships-flag.essay:
People live on ships today, for years at a time, and nobody sends a warship to stop them. To see what that does and does not give a person, it helps to understand the flag.

Every ship on the high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, belongs to a country in legal terms. The flag state is the country whose flag the ship flies and whose register lists it. The system comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Nobody owns the open sea, so without some link to a country no law would reach what happens on a ship there. Under Article 90 every country, including one with no coast, may sail ships under its flag. Under Article 91 each country sets its own conditions for its flag, and there must be a "genuine link" between the country and the ship. Under Article 92(1) a ship may fly one flag only, and on the high seas only the flag state has legal power over it, except in cases set by treaty or by UNCLOS. Article 92(2) says a ship using two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having no nationality.

The register works a little like a passport for the vessel, with duties attached. Article 94 requires the flag state to keep a register and enforce rules on seaworthiness, crew and safety. Article 97 says that after a collision, only the flag state or the person's own country may bring criminal charges. Article 98 says each flag state must require captains to rescue people in danger at sea. Article 99 says any slave who reaches any ship, under any flag, is free by that fact. Open registers accept foreign-owned ships for a fee, which is why The World flies the flag of the Bahamas although it is managed from Florida. Each register sets its own limits. Liberia, for example, asks for a waiver and a willing inspection body for vessels over 20 years old.

A flag issued by a place no other country recognizes gives no protection. Article 110 lets a warship board a foreign ship if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality. The ground that matters for self-declared flags is Article 110(1)(d), having no nationality. The ship appears open to being treated that way, although the treaty does not mention unrecognized flags. US law, for one, calls a vessel "without nationality" in several situations, including when the country named denies the registry, and applies its drug law to such vessels (46 USC 70502). Full protection from boarding by other countries applies only to warships and government ships not used for trade, under Articles 95 and 96.

Registering is the easy route. Suppose a group buys a used cruise ship and registers it. They live under that country's law on board, and it can remove them from its register. A ship can only be sovereign in the legal sense if a country stands behind it, which brings the project back to the need for recognition by other countries. The first test comes from insurers, as MS Satoshi shows. Ocean Builders bought a 1991 cruise ship in 2020 to anchor in the Gulf of Panama. Protection and indemnity insurance, the liability cover owners need against claims at sea, was not available. The company said the closest offer was a $1 million premium for $5 million of cover. It asked Panama to class the ship as non-seagoing, which would have removed about 32 of 35 treaties, and Panama refused because it had an engine and a flag. Without insurance there could be no crew, which meant losing class, the safety rating from an inspection body, and then the flag. The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020.

Maintenance and money come next. Villa Vie Odyssey was a 30-year-old ship sold as a home, with cabins from $99,999 plus monthly fees. It sat for months in a Belfast yard before sailing on 30 September 2024. On 26 October 2026 at Sihanoukville in Cambodia, the chief executive told residents to leave because the company could not secure fuel, and more than 200 went ashore. Residents held a contract with a company, so their home depended on that company's money. Life at Sea Cruises sold a three-year voyage with no ship and cancelled in November 2023. By January 2024 only four passengers had refunds, and 78 customers asked US prosecutors to investigate about $16 million in deposits. How that ended is not known. Blueseed, a startup ship planned off California to avoid work visas, never raised the $18 million it needed. Freedom Ship, a plan for 80,000 people, has seen its estimate rise from $6 billion to as much as $20 billion, and Pangeos, at $8 billion, remains a design. MS The World is the working model. It was completed in 2002 and has 165 residences owned by residents, who elect an advisory board.

Women on Waves, a Dutch group, takes women to international waters to give abortion pills under the law of its Dutch flag and a Dutch permit. Portuguese warships blocked it in 2004, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in February 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression. Guatemala's army blocked the pier within 24 hours of docking. A flag gives no right to enter a port.

Coastal states have also learned to reach ships through the shore. Radio Mercur broadcast to Denmark until a 1962 law banned supporting it. Radio Nord flew Nicaragua's flag until Sweden pressed Nicaragua, and moved to Panama, and then Sweden banned selling its advertising. It closed in 1962. Radio Veronica and Radio North Sea International, whose ship Mebo II was firebombed in 1971, closed under a Dutch law of 1974. Radio Caroline kept going from international waters after Britain's 1967 Act made it illegal for British subjects to supply or advertise on it, until fuel and supplies ran out in 1990. The gambling ship SS Rex, off Santa Monica, won a court fight over how to measure a bay, and in 1939 California's Attorney General, Earl Warren, raided it as a public nuisance. The broadcasting laws left the ships alone and went after the people on land who supplied them and sold their advertising. Sea Shepherd adds another warning. In 2013 a US appeals court called its attacks on whalers piracy, holding that "private ends" means more than money, and piracy opens a ship to any warship regardless of flag.

The United States still taxes its citizens wherever they live under Cook v. Tait, and banks report accounts. A resident arriving in port falls under that port's law, and specialist medical care means going ashore. A child born at sea normally takes nationality from the parents. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which few countries have joined, treats the birth as happening in the flag country only if the child would otherwise be stateless.

A common misunderstanding is that a flag creates a country. A flag gives a ship a nationality, and a government can withdraw it, which is why Swedish pressure on Nicaragua pushed Radio Nord's owners to Panama. Another is that a registered ship is lawless at sea, when the flag state's law applies. The workable version is an ordinary registered ship run by a solid company, with a private ownership agreement, as The World has. Living there is estimated as very achievable, while recognition as a state is estimated at close to nothing, because residents trade independence for stability.
